                      fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center", dpi = 72)

A fitted lag sequential model is an estimate, not a finding. The adjusted
residual tests each transition against independence, but that test rests on
large-sample assumptions that sequential data can violate: transitions within
one sequence are not independent observations, and a few long or atypical
sequences can carry a large share of the table. A claim about a transition
therefore needs evidence matched to its scope. A claim about one edge needs
an estimate of how precisely that edge is known; a claim that a significant
edge is real needs to survive the loss of part of the sample; a claim about
the whole network needs to reproduce in independent halves of the data; and
a claim that the structure exceeds chance needs a null that does not rest on
the residual's approximation.

`lagdynamics` pairs each kind of claim with a procedure. All of them take the
fitted model as their first argument and are read with `transitions()`, the
same verb that reads the fit.

| Claim | Evidence | Function |
|---|---|---|
| a transition is precisely estimated | edge-level uncertainty | `certainty_lsa()`, `bootstrap_lsa()` |
| a significant transition is not fragile | robustness to case loss | `stability_lsa()` |
| the whole network is reproducible | split-half reliability | `reliability_lsa()` |
| the structure exceeds chance | an empirical null | `permute_lsa()` |

Differences between groups are a claim of their own and are covered in
[Comparing groups](https://pak.dynasite.org/lagdynamics/articles/group-comparison.html).

## Data

`engagement` records the weekly engagement state of 138 students over 15
weeks; two rows are entirely missing, so the model uses 136 sequences.

- **Sequence:** each row is one student.
- **Order:** the column order, weeks 1 to 15.
- **State:** `Active`, `Average`, or `Disengaged`.

The student is the unit that all resampling procedures below draw, drop, or
split, because the transitions of one student are dependent.

```{r fit}
library(lagdynamics)
fit <- lsa(engagement)
transitions(fit, significant = TRUE, sort = "strength")
```

Seven of the nine transitions are significant: the three self-transitions are
over-represented, and the four moves into or out of `Active` are avoided. The
procedures below ask how much of this survives scrutiny.

## Edge uncertainty

A claim about one transition requires an estimate of how much it could vary.
`certainty_lsa()` derives that uncertainty analytically: each state's
outgoing transitions are modelled as Dirichlet-Multinomial, which gives a
posterior mean, a credible interval, and a certainty decision for every
transition probability without resampling.

```{r certainty}
cert <- certainty_lsa(fit)
cert
transitions(cert)
```

The persistence `Active -> Active` is pinned down tightly: a probability of
0.698 with a 95% credible interval from 0.661 to 0.731. Two edges are not
classed as stable. `Disengaged -> Active` has an interval from 0.088 to
0.158 around a probability of 0.120, wide relative to its size because
`Disengaged` is the least visited source state, and `Active -> Disengaged`
(0.035, interval 0.023 to 0.051) is equally imprecise relative to its size.
A residual can be large while the probability behind it is still uncertain,
which is why both are reported.

`bootstrap_lsa()` reaches the same question by resampling. It draws students
with replacement, refits the model on each resample, and records a
percentile interval for the count, the residual, the probability, and
Yule's Q of every edge (Efron, 1979). Resampling whole sequences preserves
the dependence within each student that the analytic model ignores, so the
bootstrap is preferred when students may differ systematically. The seed is
set once here and governs every resampling procedure in this article; the
bootstrap draws 500 resamples.

```{r bootstrap}
set.seed(2026)
boot <- bootstrap_lsa(fit, R = 500)
boot
transitions(boot, significant = TRUE) |> head(4)
```

Seven of the nine edges are stable under the bootstrap: their residual
interval excludes zero. `transitions(boot, significant = TRUE)` keeps
those seven, and the first four are shown. The residual of
`Active -> Active` ranges from 18.8 to 24.31 across resamples, far from
zero. Its probability interval, 0.640 to 0.748, is wider than the analytic
credible interval (0.661 to 0.731) because resampling students carries the
variation between students that the Dirichlet-Multinomial model treats as
absent. `Disengaged -> Active` shows why the two procedures answer different
questions: its residual interval (-12.6 to -8.35) is firmly negative, so the
avoidance itself is not in doubt, while its probability (0.080 to 0.164)
remains imprecise.

The bootstrap forest shows the interval of every edge at once.

```{r forest, fig.height = 5}
plot(boot)
```

Each spoke is one edge: the square is the bootstrap estimate of the adjusted
residual, the bar its 95% interval, and the dashed ring the null value of
zero. The seven significant edges lie clearly inside or outside the ring,
over-represented edges outside and avoided edges inside, while the two grey,
non-significant edges, `Average -> Disengaged` and
`Disengaged -> Average`, sit on it. No significant edge has an interval that
reaches the null.

## Robustness to case loss

`stability_lsa()` repeatedly drops a share of the students, refits, and
records the fraction of replicates in which each edge is significant
(`stability`). By default it keeps 80% of the students per replicate and
flags an edge as stable when it is significant in at least 95% of
replicates. The call below runs 200 replicates.

```{r stability}
stab <- stability_lsa(fit, R = 200)
stab
transitions(stab)
```

None of the 200 replicates failed, and all seven significant edges remain
significant in every replicate (stability 1.000), so the significance
pattern does not depend on particular students. Of the two non-significant
edges, `Average -> Disengaged` is significant in 0.5% of replicates and
`Disengaged -> Average` in 25.5%: the latter has a residual of -1.7, close
to the threshold, and crosses it in some subsamples. Its non-significance is
therefore a borderline result rather than a firm absence of effect.

## Reproducibility of the whole network

`reliability_lsa()` raises the claim from one edge to the whole network. It
splits the students at random into two halves, fits a model to each, and
correlates the two vectors of edge weights (transition probabilities by
default); the distribution of this split-half correlation over replicates
measures how reproducible the network is within the sample (Epskamp,
Borsboom, & Fried, 2018). The call below draws 100 splits.

```{r reliability}
rel <- reliability_lsa(fit, R = 100)
rel
as.data.frame(rel, what = "summary")
```

The mean split-half correlation of the transition probabilities is 0.966
(sd 0.034), with 95% of replicates between 0.866 and 0.998: two independent
halves of the students produce nearly the same network. The printout and
the summary table also report failed replicates, splits in which a half
could not be fitted (for example because a state is absent from it); here
the count is 0 of 100, so the correlation rests on every split drawn. A
non-zero count is reported rather than silently dropped and is read before
the correlation.

## An empirical null

`permute_lsa()` builds the null of no sequential structure by shuffling the
order of states within each student and refitting. Shuffling within a
sequence keeps every student's mix of states, so the null asks whether a
transition is more or less frequent than that mix implies, and the p-value
does not depend on the residual's large-sample approximation. The call below
runs 500 permutations, so the smallest attainable p-value is 1/501.

```{r permute}
perm <- permute_lsa(fit, R = 500)
perm
transitions(perm)
```

Seven edges are significant under the permutation null, as under the
residual test, but not the same seven. Five edges reach p = 0.00200, the
smallest value 500 permutations can produce. `Disengaged -> Active`, with
a residual of -10.5, has a permutation p-value of 0.078 and is not
significant. Shuffling within each student keeps that student's mix of
states, so a student who is rarely both disengaged and active produces few
such moves under the null as well; the avoidance is explained by which
students are disengaged, not by the order of their weeks. The reverse holds
for `Disengaged -> Average`: its residual (-1.7) is not significant, but its
permutation p-value is 0.022, so disengaged students move to `Average` less
often than their own mix of states implies. `Disengaged -> Active` is also
the edge whose probability `certainty_lsa()` did not class as stable, so the
claim that disengaged students avoid becoming active rests on the residual
alone and is not reported as an established sequential effect.

## When to use which

- **A descriptive reading of a transition** needs only the fit:
  `transitions(fit)`.
- **How precisely a transition is known:** `certainty_lsa()` when sequences
  are homogeneous and a fast analytic answer is enough, `bootstrap_lsa()`
  when sequences may differ.
- **Whether a significant transition depends on particular cases:**
  `stability_lsa()`.
- **Whether the whole network reproduces:** `reliability_lsa()`.
- **Whether a transition exceeds what each sequence's own mix of states
  implies:** `permute_lsa()`.
- **Whether two groups differ:** `compare_lsa()` and `bayes_compare_lsa()`,
  in [Comparing groups](https://pak.dynasite.org/lagdynamics/articles/group-comparison.html).

A transition that is significant, precisely estimated, stable under case
loss, and beyond the permutation null is the kind to report as a finding.

## References

Efron, B. (1979). Bootstrap methods: Another look at the jackknife.
*Annals of Statistics, 7*(1), 1-26.

Epskamp, S., Borsboom, D., & Fried, E. I. (2018). Estimating psychological
networks and their accuracy: A tutorial paper. *Behavior Research Methods,
50*(1), 195-212.
